stack.title: Call stack
stack.hint: LIFO — one function at a time

classic.label: setTimeout + Promise
narrations: Line 1 runs synchronously — 'A' is logged.
setTimeout hands its callback to the Web APIs.
Even with a 0 ms delay, the callback waits in the macrotask queue.
The .then handler is scheduled on the microtask queue.
Microtasks always run before the next macrotask.
Line 11 runs — 'D' is logged. Sync code still first.
Call stack is empty. The loop drains microtasks next.
The .then callback runs — 'C' is logged.
Now the macrotask fires — 'B' is logged. Final order: A, D, C, B.

promises.label: Chained promises
narrations: A resolved promise is created.
The first .then is scheduled as a microtask.
Sync code runs first — 'sync' is logged.
Stack empty. Microtask queue drains.
'start' is logged; returning 'next' schedules the next .then.
The second .then joins the microtask queue immediately.
'next' is logged. Order: sync, start, next.

nested.label: Microtasks starving tasks
narrations: Timer scheduled.
Timer callback waits in the macrotask queue.
chain() is queued as a microtask.
Call stack empties. Microtasks always run first.
'micro' is logged.
chain() re-schedules itself — new microtask.
Loop drains microtasks before touching the timer again…
'micro' is logged again — the timer keeps waiting.
This is how a runaway promise chain can starve macrotasks.

hero.subtitle: Software engineer, named after ζ Ursae Majoris — the second star from the tip of the Big Dipper's handle. Naked-eye visible, part of a sextuple system. I got the name; the sky got the naming rights.

origin.title: First, I tried to make sense of the world in numbers.
origin.body: Nineteen, enrolled in Statistics & Finance at the University of Padua. I was learning to see the world as distributions and confidence intervals. It made sense on paper. It didn't move me.

leap.title: Then I left.
leap.body: Twenty years old. Working-holiday visa. One backpack, and one country that seemed impossibly far away. I stayed in Australia for a year. Four more countries followed. Somewhere between a night bus and a farm on the other side of the world, I learned that curiosity teaches faster than a lecture hall.

pivot.title: A European Technical Degree, and a Trojan horse.
pivot.body: Back in Italy. Machina Lonati, a two-year technical program in Digital Marketing. I signed up for the marketing. I stayed for what came after — the more I learned about how websites converted, the more I wanted to know how they were built.

firstCommit.title: The small thrill of shipping something real.
firstCommit.body: First internship. WordPress themes, custom landing pages, occasional jQuery — the workhorse stack of small studios. I also brokered a deal with a doctor who wanted a platform: turnover went up 20% that quarter. That was the moment I understood the leverage of code.

engineering.title: Where 'stakeholder alignment' stopped sounding like a joke.
engineering.body: GIS + JavaScript + Python. I built a geolocation dashboard for a European automotive brand, and a location-analytics tool for a global F&B client that landed in the internal top 5%. Two years of learning to translate messy human problems into structured queries.

matures.title: The hardest problems in engineering are rarely the code.
matures.body: Two years shipping React and Node across cross-disciplinary teams — an automotive management platform, then something for an Italian telco supplier. Cross-team communication became a skill I could point to. Tests, real tests, became a habit.

now.title: React, Next, and notarized on-chain.
now.body: A full restyling of a luxury watch marketplace notarized on Algorand — Core Web Vitals up 10%. A custom platform for a medical society — 95% of requested features shipped in an MVP measured in months, not quarters. In 2023–24 I studied blockchain properly at Masterz, so the on-chain work has real ground under it.

offKeyboard.title: I collect two kinds of horizons.
offKeyboard.body: The ones covered in snow, and the ones that stretch across water. Skiing since I could stand. Swimming since I could hold my breath. Both remind me that fluency is the same everywhere — deep practice, made to look effortless.
offKeyboard.waterSub: since I could hold my breath

family.title: My brother, Akela.
family.body: He runs a kitchen the way I try to run a codebase — with an obsession for the small things. Last year I spent six months with him in Melbourne, mostly in his kitchen, occasionally on the floor at his private events. Turns out mise en place teaches the same lesson as a good deploy: everything in its place, and then the calm.

stack.title: What I build with, today.
stack.body: Preferences, not dogma. I reach for what makes the next teammate's Tuesday morning easier.

closures.title: Closures, unpacked.
closures.description: A closure is a function bundled with the scope it was born in. That's what lets callbacks 'remember' their surroundings — and it's why the loop-with-var has that famous bug.
closures.idleNarration: Pick a scenario, then press Run to walk through it.

basic.label: Basic capture
narrations: Nothing has run yet — just the global scope, holding the declaration of outer.
const f = outer() calls outer. A fresh outer() scope is pushed on the stack.
const secret = 42 adds secret to outer's scope.
inner is created inside outer. It carries a reference to outer's scope.
outer returns inner. Normally its scope would vanish — but f now holds a reference to inner, which holds outer's scope. It stays alive as 'captured'.
f() runs the captured inner. A new inner() scope is pushed, linked to the captured outer.
return secret looks up secret — not found locally, so it walks the chain to the captured outer, and reads 42.
inner returns 42. The console prints 42. That's a closure.

counter.label: Shared counter
narrations: makeCounter() runs. Its scope pushes on the stack.
let count = 0 binds count in makeCounter's scope.
An object with inc and get is created. Both arrow functions capture makeCounter's scope.
makeCounter returns. Its scope is held by two closures now — it stays as 'captured'.
c.inc() runs. ++count bumps count from 0 to 1 in the captured scope.
c.inc() runs again. count goes from 1 to 2 — same scope, same binding.
c.get() reads count from the shared captured scope: 2.
console.log prints 2. Both closures agree on the same private state — that's the module pattern.

forVar.label: for + var (the bug)
narrations: for (var i = 0; ...) starts. Because it's var, i lives in the surrounding scope — not in each iteration.
setTimeout schedules a callback. Its arrow captures the surrounding scope — the one holding i.
i++ → i is now 1. Second setTimeout schedules another callback, capturing the same scope.
i++ → i is 2. Third setTimeout, third callback in the queue — still capturing the same scope.
i++ → i is 3. The condition fails, the loop exits. But i in the shared scope is now stuck at 3.
The stack is empty. The event loop reaches for the task queue.
Callback 1 fires. It reads i from the shared scope — 3. Logs 3.
Callback 2 fires. Same shared scope, same i — logs 3.
Callback 3 fires. Logs 3. All three saw the same binding, at the same moment in time.

forLet.label: for + let (the fix)
narrations: Same loop, but with let. let is block-scoped — each iteration gets its own fresh scope.
Iteration 0: a new block scope is created with its own i = 0. setTimeout captures it.
The iteration ends. Normally the block scope would vanish — but the queued callback holds it. It stays as 'captured'.
Iteration 1: a brand-new block scope with i = 1. Second setTimeout captures this one.
That scope is captured too. Now two independent scopes are being kept alive.
Iteration 2: fresh scope, i = 2. Third setTimeout captures it.
The loop exits. Three captured scopes are still around, each with its own i.
Callback 1 fires. It reads from iteration 0's scope — 0. Logs 0.
Callback 2 fires. Iteration 1's scope — 1.
Callback 3 fires. Iteration 2's scope — 2. Three separate memories, one per iteration.
